Should call register with deleteOnExit? The simple approach: if file.isDirectory() then delete recursively then schedule? But scheduling directory recursively will require deleteOnExit for each file. Implementation: implement a helper that registers all files via deleteOnExit. In Java, File.deleteOnExit() registers full path; deleteOnExit removes after normal exit. For directories, deleteOnExit will only delete if empty, but we want delete directory after its contents are removed. So we need to delete contents on exit in reverse order? The Java Framework's deleteOnExit will delete from leaf to root, as each file is registered in order. It will delete directories after contents. So to delete a directory entirely, we need to register all files and subdirectories in order; to ensure directories are after files, we can traverse tree and call deleteOnExit on all files and then directories. If we call deleteOnExit on file then register subdirectories first? Actually File.deleteOnExit registers at system exit. On exit it deletes in reverse order of registration. So to delete a directory after its contents, register contents first then directory. The standard Java method for deleteOnExit() for directory may not work if only the outer directory is registered; but as per Java's DeleteOnExit, it will attempt to delete the directory and will succeed only if empty; if it is not empty, deletion fails. Example: typical library uses: If file is directory, we call register for each subdirectory after the files. But simpler: recursion: we traverse depth-first, and for each file, call deleteOnExit(); for each directory, we register after its contents: in DFS, we can collect all directories then deleteOnExit them after recursion.

For directories, deleteOnExit will only delete if empty, but we want delete directory after its contents are removed. So we need to delete contents on exit in reverse order? The Java Framework's deleteOnExit will delete from leaf to root, as each file is registered in order. It will delete directories after contents. So to delete a directory entirely, we need to register all files and subdirectories in order; to ensure directories are after files, we can traverse tree and call deleteOnExit on all files and then directories. If we call deleteOnExit on file then register subdirectories first? Actually File.deleteOnExit registers at system exit. On exit it deletes in reverse order of registration. So to delete a directory after its contents, register contents first then directory. The standard Java method for deleteOnExit() for directory may not work if only the outer directory is registered; but as per Java's DeleteOnExit, it will attempt to delete the directory and will succeed only if empty; if it is not empty, deletion fails. Example: typical library uses: If file is directory, we call register for each subdirectory after the files.
